front: Problem
back: A situation in which an existing system or process isn't working as it should, for example because it causes errors, delays or extra cost.
mistake: A problem needs something that is currently falling short. If the current system works well and the goal is to gain something new, it's an opportunity, not a problem.

front: Need
back: Something an individual or organisation requires but doesn't yet have, such as a way to meet a new legal reporting duty.
mistake: A need doesn't depend on anything going wrong. It can arise when a new obligation applies that the organisation has never had to meet, even though its current system works well.

front: Opportunity
back: A chance to gain an advantage or do something new, often opened up by new technology or a new market, even when the current system works well.

front: What four reasons for undertaking a software development project does the study design list?
back:
- increasing productivity and efficiency
- reducing costs
- identifying opportunities to address gaps in the market
- meeting organisational objectives or needs

They apply to individuals as well as organisations.
mistake: The list isn't the only accepted answer. On the 2025 case study, examiners also credited fewer human errors and better communication, which the case raised, so read each reason from the scenario.

front: Why might an individual, rather than an organisation, undertake a software development project?
back: To solve a personal problem or automate a task they do often; to create a product they can sell or share; to meet the needs of a group they belong to, such as a club; or to build their skills and portfolio.

front: Problem versus opportunity
back:
| | Problem | Opportunity |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Current system | Falling short (errors, delays, cost) | May work well |
| Aim | Fix what isn't working | Gain an advantage or offer something new |
| Example | Paper bookings cause double-bookings | Online booking would let a clinic take bookings after hours |

front: A café whose handwritten orders are often misread by kitchen staff has {{a problem}}; a café that could sell meal subscriptions online, which no local rival offers, has {{an opportunity}}.
back: A problem means the current process falls short. An opportunity means gaining something new, even when nothing is broken.

front: Why should a software project start by identifying the problem, need or opportunity?
back: It states why the solution is being built. That purpose shapes the brief, guides which data is collected and which requirements matter, and gives criteria for judging later whether the solution succeeded.
mistake: The reason for a project isn't 'to build an app'. The app is the means; the reason is what the organisation or individual gains from it, such as fixing a problem, cutting costs or meeting a need.

front: Brief
back: A short document, written at the start of a project, that outlines the problem, need or opportunity and the proposed solution. It names the proposed users and the programming languages to be used, and shows that the project is feasible and original.

front: Which features of a brief does the study design list?
back:
- problem/need/opportunity outline
- proposed users
- programming languages to be used
- feasibility (whether the project is achievable with the time, skills and resources available)
- originality (how the idea differs from existing solutions)
mistake: Stopping at the problem and the users misses three features: the list also includes the programming languages to be used, feasibility and originality.

front: Brief versus software requirements specification (SRS)
back:
| | Brief | SRS |
|:--|:--|:--|
| When | Start of the project | After data collection and analysis |
| Detail | Short and high level | Detailed and precise |
| Purpose | Explain why a solution is wanted | Set out what the solution must do, for design and testing |
mistake: A brief isn't a short SRS. It comes before analysis, so it can't yet list the detailed requirements that analysis produces.

front: Why is a brief usually written in plain, non-technical language?
back: Its readers include the client and other stakeholders, not only developers, and they must be able to confirm that it describes their situation and goals correctly before analysis begins. It still names technical choices such as the programming language to be used.

front: What kind of content doesn't belong in a brief?
back: Design and development detail, such as mock-ups, pseudocode, data dictionaries, testing tables and a full list of requirements. These are produced later, once analysis has worked out what the solution must do.
mistake: Putting screen layouts or code in a brief jumps ahead of analysis. A brief outlines the proposed solution and names the programming language to be used, but the detailed design comes after analysis.

front: A brief explains {{why}} a solution is wanted and outlines the proposed solution; the detail of {{how}} the solution will work is decided after analysis.
back: A brief can name the programming language to be used, but screen layouts, algorithms and data structures belong to the design stage.

front: How does a developer use a brief at the start of analysis?
back: As the starting point. It identifies the stakeholders to collect data from and the issues to ask them about. The requirements, constraints and scope found through that data collection are then documented in the SRS.

front: Why should a brief identify the proposed users?
back: The users' characteristics, such as their skills, age, devices and working conditions, shape which data is collected from them and later requirements such as usability.

front: Dependency
back: A link between two tasks in which one task can't start until the other (its predecessor) has finished.
mistake: Two tasks drawn one after the other aren't necessarily dependent. A dependency exists only when one task needs the other to finish first.

front: A task on the critical path finishes two days late. What happens to the project's finish date, and why?
back: The project finishes two days late, unless later critical tasks are shortened. The task is part of the longest chain, so the delay pushes back every later task in that chain and the finish date.
mistake: Shortening or removing a task that is not on the critical path does not win back a critical-path delay. Record the delay by extending the late task's time frame and rescheduling every task that depends on it.

front: Tasks that don't depend on each other can run {{concurrently}}, which can shorten the project; tasks linked by a dependency must run in {{sequence}}.
back: Concurrent tasks overlap on the timeline. Sequenced tasks run one after another because each needs the previous one finished.
mistake: Tasks are not sequenced by the order they happen to be listed in, or by a guess at what comes first. Each task is placed after the tasks it depends on: a successor starts only once its predecessor has finished.

front: How do you find the critical path and the minimum project duration from a set of tasks and their dependencies?
back: Trace every chain of dependent tasks from the project's start to its finish and add up each chain's durations. The chain with the largest total is the critical path, and that total is the minimum project duration.
mistake: Adding every task's duration gives the project length only if no tasks overlap. Tasks that run concurrently are counted once, through the longest chain.

front: Critical task versus non-critical task
back:
| | Critical task | Non-critical task |
|:--|:--|:--|
| On the critical path? | Yes | No |
| If it is delayed | The project finishes later by the same amount | It can be delayed a limited time before the finish date moves |
mistake: A non-critical task can still delay the project if its delay is long enough to make its chain the longest one.

front: Critical path
back: The longest chain of dependent tasks, by total duration, from a project's start to its finish. Its length is the shortest time the whole project can take, so a delay to any task on it pushes back the finish date unless the plan is adjusted.
mistake: The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks, not the shortest one, and not simply the tasks that seem most important.

front: Gantt chart
back: A project management chart that shows each task as a bar along a timeline, so its start, duration and finish can be read off. It also shows how tasks are sequenced, the dependencies between them, milestones and the critical path, and it is updated during the project to monitor and document progress.
mistake: Asked how a Gantt chart monitors progress, don't describe what it looks like. Explain updating it with actual progress and comparing that with the plan, such as spotting a delay on the critical path.

front: Milestone
back: A significant point in a project, such as the completion of a stage of the problem-solving methodology (design finished, so development can begin), used to check progress against the plan. It marks a moment rather than work, so it has no duration and is usually drawn as a diamond on a Gantt chart.
mistake: A milestone isn't a task copied from the task list. In 2025, answers that named a task with a duration as a milestone earned no marks; name a checkpoint, such as finishing a stage, and say what reaching it shows.

front: Interview versus survey
back:
| | Interview | Survey |
|:--|:--|:--|
| People reached | A few | Many, quickly |
| Depth | Detailed; follow-up questions possible | Limited to the set questions |
| Data | Mostly qualitative | Mostly quantitative (closed questions) |
| Anonymity | No | Possible |
mistake: A survey isn't better just because it reaches more people. It can't follow up a vague or surprising answer.

front: When does observation suit data collection better than an interview or a survey?
back: When the developer needs to see how a task is actually done: the real steps, workarounds, time taken and where problems occur. People often can't describe routine tasks accurately, or leave steps out.
mistake: Observation shows what people do, not what they think. It isn't the technique for finding out users' opinions or preferences.

front: State two limitations of observation as a data collection technique.
back:
Any two of:
- people may work differently when they know they're being watched
- it shows what people do, but not why, or what they would prefer
- it is time-consuming, so only a few people or sessions can be observed
- the situations of interest may not happen while the observer is there

front: Open question versus closed question
back:
| | Open question | Closed question |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Answer | In the respondent's own words | Chosen from set options (yes/no, rating scale) |
| Data | Qualitative: reasons and detail | Quantitative: easy to count and compare |
| Collating | Slow | Quick |
mistake: Closed questions aren't weaker questions. They produce data that can be counted and compared across hundreds of responses.

front: Qualitative data versus quantitative data
back: Qualitative data describes opinions, reasons and experiences in words, e.g. a receptionist's account of why bookings go wrong. Quantitative data is numerical and can be counted or measured, e.g. 68% of surveyed members rating the current system 'difficult'.

front: Why is a survey often used to collect data from a large stakeholder group, such as customers?
back: It reaches many people quickly and cheaply, including people in different places. Responses can be anonymous, which encourages honest answers, and closed questions produce data that is quick to collate and analyse.

front: Why might a developer interview a manager rather than send them a survey?
back: Managers are few and hold detailed knowledge of goals and processes. An interview allows follow-up questions and clarification, so the developer gets in-depth information that fixed survey questions would miss.

front: A large group spread across many locations suits {{a survey}}; a few people with detailed knowledge suit {{interviews}}; staff carrying out a routine process suit {{observation}}.
back: Match the technique to the stakeholder group: its size, where its members are, and whether you need opinions, detail or evidence of how a task is really done.
mistake: Naming the right technique is not enough. The reason has to come from the case: how many people are in the group, where they are, and whether follow-up questions or first-hand evidence are needed.

front: What does reliability mean as a non-functional requirement?
back: The solution performs its functions consistently and correctly whenever it is needed, without crashing or losing data. E.g. the booking system stays available throughout clinic hours.

front: What does usability mean as a non-functional requirement?
back: How easily the intended users can learn and use the solution to complete their tasks. E.g. a new receptionist can make a booking within two minutes without help.

front: What does portability mean as a non-functional requirement?
back: The solution can run on different devices, operating systems or platforms with little or no change. E.g. the app works on Android and iOS phones and in a web browser.
mistake: A platform statement such as 'the app doesn't have to run on tablets' isn't a functional requirement, because it doesn't describe something the app does. It concerns where the app works, which is portability, so it is non-functional.

front: Functional requirement versus non-functional requirement
back:
| | Functional | Non-functional |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Describes | What the solution does: its inputs, outputs, processing and validation | Qualities it must have: how well it works |
| Example | Calculate each member's annual fee | A new user can pay a fee in under two minutes |
| Checked by | Testing that outputs are correct | Measuring against a stated target |
mistake: A number doesn't make a requirement non-functional. 'Staff can search orders from the past three years' still says what the solution does, so it is functional; a requirement is non-functional when it describes a quality, such as reliability or usability.

front: Why should a non-functional requirement be measurable?
back: So it can be tested during development and checked in evaluation. 'The app should be user-friendly' can't be checked; 'a new user can book a court in under two minutes without help' can.
mistake: Words like 'user-friendly', 'fast' or 'reliable' on their own aren't requirements a developer can test. Add a measurable target.

front: 'The program must email each client an invoice' is a {{functional}} requirement; 'the program must stay available during all opening hours' is a {{non-functional}} requirement concerning {{reliability}}.
back: Functional requirements state what the solution does; non-functional requirements state qualities it must have, such as reliability, usability and portability.

front: Functional requirement
back: A requirement that states something the solution must do: accept particular inputs, produce particular outputs, or carry out a function such as calculating, sorting or validating data. For example, 'calculate each member's annual fee' or 'reject a booking date that has already passed'.
mistake: A number doesn't make a requirement non-functional. 'Produce a report covering up to 10 years of bookings' is still something the solution does, so it is functional.

front: Non-functional requirement
back: A requirement describing a quality attribute of the solution (how well it works) rather than a task it performs. The study design's examples are usability, reliability, portability, robustness and maintainability; for example, 'a new receptionist can make a booking without any training'.
mistake: A feature isn't non-functional just because it concerns users or the screen. 'Staff can print a receipt' is something the solution does (functional); non-functional requirements are qualities such as reliability or usability.

front: Give an example of an economic constraint on a software project.
back: A limit on cost or time; the problem-solving methodology counts both as economic. E.g. the club can spend no more than $6000 on development, which may rule out paid libraries or a second developer; or the program must be ready before the season starts.
mistake: Economic constraints aren't only about money. A deadline limits the time available, and time is an economic constraint too.

front: Give an example of a technical constraint on a software project.
back: A limit set by the technology available, e.g. the program must run on the clinic's existing laptops, or the clinic has only a slow, unreliable internet connection.

front: Give an example of a legal constraint on a software project.
back: A limit set by law, e.g. patients' personal and health information must be collected, stored and shared only as privacy law allows, or the solution must not use images or code without the owner's permission.

front: Why must constraints be identified during analysis, before design begins?
back: They limit which designs are possible. A design that ignores a constraint, for example one that costs more than the budget or won't run on the existing hardware, would have to be reworked. Constraints are recorded in the SRS so designers work within them.

front: 'The app must run on the school's existing Chromebooks' is {{a technical}} constraint; 'development must cost no more than $4000' is {{an economic}} constraint.
back: Technical constraints come from the hardware, software and networks available; economic constraints come from the money and time available.

front: How can a constraint shape a design decision? Give an example.
back: It rules options in or out. E.g. if the orchard's tablets often have no internet connection, the design must store records on the device and upload them later; a small budget may rule out a paid mapping library.

front: Constraint
back: A limit the solution has to be designed and built within. The study design's types are economic (cost and time), technical (e.g. processing speed, capacity, available equipment, compatibility, security), social (the users' level of expertise), legal (intellectual property, data ownership and privacy) and usability (accessibility, usefulness, ease of use).
mistake: A constraint limits how the solution can be built; it isn't a task the solution performs. 'Development must cost under $5000' is a constraint, so it doesn't belong among the functional requirements.

front: Scope versus constraint
back:
| | Scope | Constraint |
|:--|:--|:--|
| What it is | A boundary chosen for the solution | A condition that limits the solution or the project |
| Example | Will take bookings; will not take payments | Must cost less than $20 000 |
| Question it answers | What will the solution cover? | What must the project work within? |
mistake: A deadline or a budget is a constraint, not scope. Scope describes what the solution covers, not the limits it is built under.

front: Scope versus functional requirements
back:
| | Scope | Functional requirements |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Detail | High level: the main features included and those excluded | Detailed: each specific thing the solution must do |
| Example | Will record tool loans; will not manage memberships | Must list every tool that is past its due date |
| Relationship | Sets the outer limits | Every one falls inside the scope |

front: The scope of a solution is determined in the {{analysis}} stage of the problem-solving methodology and recorded in the {{software requirements specification}} (SRS).
back: Scope must be settled before design, so designers know which features to plan for and which to leave out.

front: Give three reasons why a clearly documented scope matters to a software project.
back:
Any three:
- the client and developer agree on what will be delivered
- time and cost can be estimated realistically
- requests for extra features can be recognised as scope changes
- it is clear when the solution is complete
- evaluation can judge the solution against what was agreed

front: How should a project team handle a request for a feature outside the agreed scope?
back: Treat it as a change to the scope. Record the request, assess its effect on time, cost and other tasks, and add it only if the client agrees to the change. Otherwise, leave it for a later version.
mistake: Adding a 'small' extra without assessing it is how scope creep starts. Unchecked extras draw time and effort away from the original objectives, which may then not be met; they don't simply give the client a better product.

front: What problems can a poorly defined scope cause?
back: Features nobody needs get built, requests for extras can't be recognised (scope creep), deadlines and budgets are missed, and the client and developer may disagree about whether the solution is finished.

front: Solution scope
back: The limits of what a solution, or one version of it, will cover: the features and problems it will deal with and those it won't. These limits are settled during analysis and recorded in the software requirements specification, e.g. 'version 1 takes bookings; online payment waits for version 2'.
mistake: Solution scope isn't variable scope (whether a variable is local or global). Stating what the solution will *not* do is part of defining its scope.

front: In a DFD, a process is named with a {{verb phrase}} such as *Calculate fee*, while data flows and data stores are named with {{nouns}} such as `booking_details` and *Bookings*.
back: A process does something to data, so its name is an action. A flow or a store is the data itself, so its name says what the data is.
mistake: A flow labelled `check_stock` names an action, not data. Rename it for the data that moves, such as `stock_query`.

front: State four convention errors to check for in a DFD.
back:
Any four:
- a flow between two data stores
- a flow between an external entity and a data store
- a flow between two external entities
- two flows that cross
- a process with no input or no output
- a data store with no input or no output
- an unlabelled flow, or one named with an action instead of data
mistake: An external entity never reads from or writes to a data store directly. A process must sit between them to handle the data.

front: External entity versus actor
back:
| | External entity | Actor |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Diagram | Context diagram and DFD | Use case diagram |
| Drawn as | A square or rectangle with its name inside | A stick figure or person icon with the role written above or below |
| What it is | A user or another system, outside the system, that sends or receives data | The role of a user who interacts with the system to achieve a goal |
mistake: An actor is named for a role, such as *Ticket inspector*, not for the organisation the person works for, the device they use or the system being modelled.

front: Data flow versus association (use case diagram)
back:
| | Data flow | Association |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Diagram | Context diagram and DFD | Use case diagram |
| Shows | Data moving, in the direction of the arrow | That an actor takes part in a use case |
| Label | A noun naming the data, such as `payment_details` | None needed: the line only links actor and use case |
mistake: Associations don't carry data labels. A use case diagram shows who interacts with which use case, not what data moves.

front: <<includes>> versus <<extends>>
back:
| | <<includes>> | <<extends>> |
|:--|:--|:--|
| When it runs | Every time the base use case runs | Only under a condition, as an optional addition |
| Arrow direction | From the base use case to the included one | From the extending use case to the base one |
| Example | *Place order* includes *Calculate total* | *Apply discount code* extends *Place order* |
mistake: The arrows point in opposite directions. An <<extends>> arrow points to the base use case, not away from it.

front: Context diagram
back: A Level 0 diagram of how a system exchanges data with the outside world. The whole system is one circle, each external entity (a user or another system outside it) is a labelled rectangle, and each data flow between an entity and the system is a labelled one-way arrow. Flows never run directly between two entities, and they don't cross.
mistake: A context diagram has no data stores and no internal processes: the system is a single circle. Stores and processes belong in the Level 1 data flow diagram.

front: Data flow diagram
back: A Level 1 diagram of how data moves within a system: where it comes from, how it is processed, where it is stored and where it goes. Processes are named circles, external entities are rectangles, data stores are two parallel lines with the store's name between them, and data flows are labelled one-way arrows. It should match the system's context diagram.
mistake: Data can't flow straight from an external entity into a data store, or directly between two stores or two entities; a process must sit between them. Asked to find this error in a DFD on the 2025 exam, 81% of students scored zero.

front: Use case diagram
back: A UML diagram of how users interact with a system. Actors (roles, drawn as stick figures) stand outside a labelled system boundary; use cases (ellipses) sit inside it; associations (plain lines) link actors to use cases; and dashed arrows labelled <<includes>> or <<extends>> show relationships between use cases.
mistake: An actor is a role that uses the system, such as a parking officer, not the organisation they work for, their device or the system itself. On the 2025 exam, 21% chose the organisation.

front: When in the problem-solving methodology is the SRS produced, and which stage uses it next?
back: At the end of the analysis stage, after data has been collected and the requirements identified. The design stage uses it next: designs are planned to meet its requirements, constraints and scope.

front: An SRS describes {{what}} a solution must do, not {{how}} it will be built.
back: Choices such as algorithms, pseudocode and detailed screen layouts are made later, in the design stage. Putting them in the SRS would tie designers down before the requirements are settled.
mistake: Pseudocode and algorithm choices don't belong in an SRS. They are design decisions, made after the SRS is agreed.

front: Who uses an SRS, and for what?
back:
- The client: to confirm the requirements are right before work begins
- Designers: to plan a solution that meets the requirements and constraints
- Developers and testers: to check the solution does what is required
- Evaluators: to judge whether the finished solution meets its requirements

front: Why should the client approve the SRS before design begins?
back: Approval confirms that both sides agree on what will be built. Designers can then work from settled requirements, and any later request can be recognised as a change to be costed and agreed, which limits scope creep and disputes.

front: What is a solution's technical environment, and why does the SRS describe it?
back: The hardware, operating system, network and other software the solution will run on or work alongside, such as an office's existing Windows laptops. Describing it in the SRS lets designers and developers choose tools and designs that will work there.

front: SRS versus project plan (Gantt chart)
back:
| | SRS | Project plan |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Describes | What the solution must do and the conditions it must meet | The tasks needed to produce it, with durations, order and dependencies |
| Used to | Design, test and evaluate the solution | Schedule and track the project |
mistake: The SRS doesn't schedule the project. It may record a deadline as a constraint, but the tasks, durations and dependencies that meet the deadline belong in the project plan.

front: A draft SRS lists only what the solution must do. Why is that not enough?
back: It doesn't say how well the solution must perform (non-functional requirements such as usability or reliability) or what limits it must work within (constraints such as budget or existing hardware). A design could provide every function yet still be unacceptable.
mistake: Non-functional requirements aren't optional extras. A solution that works but is too slow or too hard to use doesn't meet its requirements.

front: In Australia, when does program code become protected by copyright?
back: Automatically, as soon as it is written down or saved. No registration, fee or © symbol is needed.
mistake: Code doesn't need to be registered to be protected. Australia has no copyright register; IP Australia handles patents, trade marks and designs, not copyright.

front: Does copyright protect the idea behind a program, or the program's code?
back: The code: the way the program is expressed. Copyright doesn't protect the underlying idea or functionality, so another developer may build a similar program by writing their own code.
mistake: Building an app with the same features as a rival's isn't copyright infringement. Copying the rival's code, graphics or text is.

front: Code written by an employee versus code written by a contractor
back:
| | Employee | Contractor |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Default copyright owner | The employer, when the code is written as part of the job | The contractor who wrote it |
| How the client gains ownership | The employer already owns it | Through a written contract that assigns the copyright |
mistake: Paying a contractor doesn't by itself transfer copyright. Unless the contract assigns it in writing, the contractor keeps ownership of the code.

front: A developer adds an open-source library to a client's program. What must they do?
back: Follow the library's licence. Open-source code is still protected by copyright; its licence gives permission to use it on conditions, such as keeping the copyright notice and, under some licences, releasing changes under the same licence.
mistake: Open source doesn't mean free of conditions. Using the code without meeting its licence terms can infringe the owner's copyright.

front: Personal information
back: Information or an opinion about an identified person, or about a person who can reasonably be identified from it, such as a name, address, date of birth or driver licence number.
mistake: Information doesn't need a name to be personal. A driver licence number or an email address can be enough to identify someone.

front: List four ways a program can be designed to protect the privacy of the personal information it handles.
back:
Any four:
- collect only the information needed for its purpose
- tell users what is collected and why
- use it only for the purpose it was collected for
- restrict access to it and encrypt it when stored
- let users view and correct their own information
- delete or de-identify it when it is no longer needed

front: In Australia, the {{Copyright Act 1968}} (Cwlth) protects program code as a literary work, and the {{Privacy Act 1988}} (Cwlth) sets rules for handling personal information through the Australian Privacy Principles.
back: Copyright law covers who may copy and use code. Privacy law covers how personal information is collected, used, stored and disclosed. The Privacy Act applies to Australian Government agencies and many private organisations.

front: Intellectual property
back: Creations of the mind, such as program code, designs, written works and brand names, that the law lets their creators or owners control and profit from. In Australia, program code is protected automatically by copyright under the Copyright Act 1968 (Cwlth).
mistake: Code isn't free to reuse just because it is publicly visible online. It is still someone's intellectual property: check its licence and acknowledge its source.

front: What makes a good file naming convention for a software project?
back: Names that are consistent, descriptive and sortable: the same order of parts every time, the project and document named, dates written as YYYY-MM-DD, a version number, and no spaces or special characters. For example, `2026-05-04_bookingapp_srs_v1.2.docx`.
mistake: 'final' isn't a version. Files are often changed after they are called final, which leads to names like `srs_final2_FINAL.docx`.

front: Writing dates in file names as {{YYYY-MM-DD}} means that sorting the files by name also sorts them into {{date order}}.
back: Year first, then month, then day, each with a fixed number of digits, so `2026-03-09` sorts before `2026-10-02`. A day-first date such as `9-3-26` doesn't sort correctly.

front: Version numbers in file names versus a version control system
back:
| | Version numbers in file names | Version control system |
|:--|:--|:--|
| How versions are kept | Manually, by saving a new copy, e.g. `booking_v1.3.py` | Recorded each time a change is committed |
| Records | Only the order of versions | Every change, with its author, date and message |
| Allows | Going back to a saved copy | Comparing versions, combining developers' work and rolling back |
mistake: Numbered file names are a simple, manual form of version control, but they rely on people remembering to save a new copy, and they can't show who changed what or combine two developers' work. A version control system records each committed change with its author and can merge developers' work.

front: Why should a software project keep versions of its files?
back:
- The team can roll back to an earlier working version if a change breaks the program
- Versions can be compared to find when a bug appeared
- Everyone knows which version is current
- Developers don't overwrite each other's work
mistake: Saving over the same file each time isn't versioning: the earlier working copy is gone. Keeping versions isn't a backup either; it lets the team roll back to a working version, while a backup is a separate copy kept in case the data is lost.

front: Backup versus archive
back:
| | Backup | Archive |
|:--|:--|:--|
| What it is | A copy of data, stored apart from the original | Data no longer used regularly, moved to storage that is accessed less often |
| Purpose | Restore the data if the original is lost | Keep it for later use or because rules require it, without slowing or filling the working system |
| Originals | Stay in place | Moved out of the working system |
mistake: An archive isn't a backup. Archived files are often the only copy, so the archive itself needs backing up.

front: Why should at least one backup be kept off-site?
back: A fire, flood or theft that destroys the original files can also destroy a backup kept in the same place. An off-site copy, such as one at another location or in cloud storage, survives a disaster at the main site.
mistake: A backup on a second drive in the same computer protects against a failed drive, but not against fire, theft, or ransomware that reaches both.

front: Full backup versus incremental backup
back:
| | Full | Incremental |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Copies | Every selected file | Only files changed since the last backup |
| Time and space | Slowest, largest | Fastest, smallest |
| To restore | The latest full backup alone | The latest full backup plus every incremental since it, in order |
mistake: An incremental backup can't restore files on its own: it needs the full backup and every incremental after it, in order. Don't confuse it with a differential backup, which holds everything changed since the last full backup, so a restore needs only the full backup and the latest differential.

front: Secure disposal
back: Destroying data so that it can't be recovered, such as by overwriting storage with data-wiping software, physically destroying drives, or shredding paper records.
mistake: Deleting a file or emptying the recycle bin doesn't reliably destroy the data. It can remain on the drive and be recovered with free tools.

front: Brainstorming
back: An ideation technique that gathers ideas connected to one central theme or concept without arranging them into any structure. It is written as a list, or drawn with the theme in the middle and each idea linked to it by a straight line. Ideas are gathered freely and judged only afterwards.
mistake: Criticising or discarding ideas during the session defeats the purpose. Judging comes afterwards, when the ideas are evaluated against criteria.

front: Mind map
back: A diagram that organises ideas into a structure around one central theme or concept. The theme sits in the middle, the main ideas branch from it on straight lines, and these branch out further into more specific ideas as needed, showing how the ideas group and connect.
mistake: A mind map isn't a flat list of ideas or a sequence of steps. The main considerations go on the first-level branches, and each detailed idea sits one level below the consideration it belongs to.

front: Mood board
back: A collection of images, colours, typography and code samples, gathered to explore possibilities for a solution and give its design a direction. Samples can be annotated to show which elements suit the solution and why.
mistake: A mood board sets the direction and style, but it doesn't lay out the solution's own screens or show where controls go. Sketches and, later, mock-ups do that.

front: How are sketches used when generating design ideas?
back: Sketches are quick, unrefined drawings, on paper or with drawing software, of how an interface could look or how parts of the solution could connect and work together. A designer can sketch several alternatives cheaply and show them to others for feedback before committing to one.

front: Sketch versus mock-up
back:
| | Sketch | Mock-up |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Typical use | Generating and comparing design ideas | Detailed design of the preferred idea |
| Detail | Quick and rough | Precise layout, annotated with fonts, colours and control types |
| Purpose | Explore options cheaply | Show developers exactly how a screen will look |

front: Brainstorming versus mind map
back:
| | Brainstorming | Mind map |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Structure | Unstructured: ideas gathered around a central theme | Structured: ideas branch from the theme, then branch further |
| Recorded as | A list, or a diagram with each idea joined straight to the theme | A diagram |
| Shows | The range of ideas | How the ideas group and connect |

A brainstorm's ideas are often sorted into a mind map afterwards.
mistake: Drawing it as a diagram doesn't make it a mind map: a brainstorm can be drawn too, with each idea joined straight to the central theme. A mind map groups the ideas under main branches that branch out further.

front: Why should a designer generate several design ideas rather than developing the first one?
back: Comparing alternatives against evaluation criteria shows which idea best meets the requirements. Settling on the first idea risks missing a better solution.
mistake: Generating design ideas isn't the same as producing the detailed design. Ideas are broad alternatives; only the chosen one is detailed with mock-ups, pseudocode and other design tools.

front: A brainstorm aims for a large {{quantity}} of ideas and {{defers judgement}} until the session ends.
back: Unusual ideas often spark better ones. Judging ideas during the session makes people hold back their suggestions.

front: Efficiency versus effectiveness
back:
| | Efficiency | Effectiveness |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Asks | How much time, cost and effort? | How well is the purpose achieved? |
| Measures | Speed, cost, effort | Accuracy, completeness, usability |
| Example | A report runs in 2 seconds, not 40 | Every total in the report is correct |
mistake: The two are independent. A solution can be efficient but ineffective (fast but inaccurate), or effective but inefficient (correct but slow).

front: Give three measures of the efficiency of a solution.
back:
- Speed: how long processing or a task takes
- Cost: how much it costs to run, such as the cost of handling its data and files
- Effort: how many steps a user needs to complete a task

front: Give three measures of the effectiveness of a solution.
back:
- Accuracy: the output is correct
- Completeness: the output includes everything required
- Usability: users can achieve their goals easily

Others in the study design's list include readability, relevance and timeliness.

front: Where do evaluation criteria come from?
back: From the solution's requirements. Criteria check how well the functional and non-functional requirements have been met, so each criterion can be traced back to what was documented and agreed with the client.
mistake: Criteria aren't invented after the solution is built. They come from the requirements agreed earlier, so the solution is judged against what the client needed.

front: What makes an evaluation criterion well written?
back: It is specific and measurable, is linked to a requirement, and says what will be checked. For example, 'A new user can complete a booking in under two minutes without help' rather than 'The app is easy to use'.
mistake: Vague criteria such as 'the program is fast' can't be judged objectively, so the evaluation becomes a matter of opinion.

front: During design, evaluation criteria are used to {{choose between design ideas}}; in the evaluation stage, the same criteria are used to judge the finished solution's {{efficiency and effectiveness}}.
back: The criteria are developed in the design stage from the requirements and refined as the solution develops. They are not replaced by a new set: the finished solution is judged against the criteria used to choose its design.

front: Evaluation criteria
back: Specific, measurable statements drawn from the solution requirements and used to judge efficiency and effectiveness. During design they are used to choose the preferred design idea; the same criteria are used again in the evaluation stage to judge how well the finished solution meets its requirements.
mistake: 'The app is good' isn't a criterion, because no evidence can show whether it has been met. 'A new booking can be made in under one minute' can be checked.

front: How does a detailed design differ from a design idea?
back: A design idea is a broad alternative, often sketched, used to compare approaches. A detailed design develops the chosen idea with design tools such as mock-ups, data dictionaries, object descriptions, IPO charts and pseudocode, setting out how it looks, how it is structured and how it works, so developers can build it.

front: Why is a detailed design produced before development starts?
back:
- The client can check the appearance and processing before any code is written
- Errors are cheaper to fix in a design than in code
- Developers get a precise specification to build from

front: Why should the names in a data dictionary match those used in the pseudocode and object descriptions?
back: So every design tool refers to each data item in the same way. Developers then use one agreed identifier and data type, which avoids confusion and errors when modules are combined.
mistake: Thinking a new name only has to say the right thing. It must also follow the design's existing convention: the 2025 examiners gave no marks for an attribute that broke the object description's camel casing.

front: What does the Field size column of a data dictionary record?
back: How large a data item can be. For a String, this is usually the maximum number of characters, e.g. 30 for a surname. It guides the width of input fields and the limits a validation check enforces. Field size is optional: every data dictionary gives at least a name and data type.

front: In an IPO chart, the {{Process}} column describes actions such as 'calculate the delivery fee', while the Input and Output columns list {{data}}.
back: Inputs and outputs are data items, such as `parcelWeight` and `deliveryFee`. The Process column (sometimes headed Processes) describes what is done to the inputs to produce the outputs.
mistake: An action such as 'calculate total' doesn't belong in the Output column. The output is the total itself; calculating it is processing.

front: A mock-up shows the {{layout and appearance}} of a screen, but it is a drawing, not a {{working}} interface.
back: Annotations add details of its appearance, such as fonts and colours, and of its structure, such as control types, default values and what each button does, so developers know exactly what to build.
mistake: A mock-up doesn't show how data moves through a system; that is the job of a data flow diagram.

front: Data dictionary versus object description
back: A **data dictionary** plans the data a module uses (such as variables, constants, objects and interface controls), giving at least each item's name and data type, often with a description, field size, validation rules or a sample. An **object description** plans one object in three sections: Name, Properties/Attributes (its data, data types optional) and Methods (its behaviours, with any parameters).
mistake: A data dictionary has no methods. Actions belong in an object description or in pseudocode.

front: How should an input control on a mock-up relate to the data dictionary or object description?
back: The data each input control captures should appear as a data item or property, with a data type that matches the control. For example, a check box is ticked or not, so it maps to a Boolean.

front: Affordance versus usability
back:
| | Affordance | Usability |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Describes | One element: whether its appearance shows how to use it | The whole solution: how easily users learn and operate it to complete their tasks, and how satisfied they are |
| Example | A raised, shaded button that looks pressable | New staff can record a sale without help |
mistake: Affordance isn't the same as usability. Good affordance is one thing that makes a solution usable, because a control's appearance tells users what they can do with it, but unclear wording or navigation can still make the solution hard to use.

front: How does security form part of a user's experience?
back: The study design's security characteristic has two parts: authentication (confirming who the user is, e.g. sign-in or a one-time code; a logout button ends the session) and data protection (keeping users' data private, e.g. no personal details shown before sign-in, encrypted storage). Users trust a solution that visibly protects them, but extra steps shouldn't make it frustrating to use.
mistake: A screen that shows private details to anyone who opens it is a security weakness, however easy it is to use. Login and logout features are what show users that their account and data are protected.

front: Interoperability versus portability
back: **Interoperability**: the solution exchanges data with other systems, e.g. its bookings can be imported into a calendar app. **Portability**: the solution runs on different platforms, e.g. on Android, on iOS and in a web browser.
mistake: Running on both Android and iOS is portability, not interoperability. Portability is a non-functional requirement, not one of the four UX characteristics (affordance, interoperability, security, usability), so it earns nothing as a UX answer.

front: A "Next" option shown as flat grey text, with no border or shading, has poor {{affordance}}, because nothing in its appearance suggests it can be clicked.
back: Borders, shading, button shapes and changes on hover all signal that an element is interactive.
mistake: When users can't tell that an element can be clicked, or what it is for, the UX characteristic to improve is affordance. Contrast is a design principle, not a UX characteristic, although a quarter of students chose it for this on the 2025 exam.

front: How can adding a security feature reduce usability, and how can a designer limit the effect?
back: Features such as multi-factor authentication add steps before users reach their task. Designers can limit this, for example by remembering trusted devices or offering fingerprint sign-in, so protection stays strong with less effort.
mistake: Security and usability aren't a choice of one or the other. The aim is a design that protects users while keeping extra steps to a minimum.

front: A club's app exports its membership list as a CSV file so that the club's accounting program can import it. This improves the app's {{interoperability}}.
back: A standard, widely supported format lets data move between different programs without being retyped.

front: Affordance
back: A characteristic of user experience: how clearly an interface element's appearance shows what it does and how to use it. A raised, shaded button looks as though it can be pressed, underlined blue text looks clickable, and an empty box with a blinking cursor invites typing.
mistake: When users can't tell what the fields and buttons on a screen are for, the UX characteristic to improve is affordance, not contrast. Contrast is a design principle; a quarter of students chose it on the 2025 exam.

front: Interoperability
back: A characteristic of user experience: the solution's ability to exchange data and work with other systems, programs and devices, often through shared formats or standards such as CSV or XML. For example, a clinic's booking program passes each appointment to a text message service, which sends the patient a reminder.
mistake: Interoperability isn't portability. Working with other systems and their data is interoperability; running on different platforms with little or no change is portability.

front: Usability
back: How easily the intended users can learn and operate a solution to complete their tasks, and how satisfied they are using it; it includes ease of use and accessibility. The study design treats it as a characteristic of user experience and as a design principle, and it can also be a non-functional requirement or a constraint.

front: Alignment
back: Placing elements so their edges or centres line up along shared lines. It gives a screen a clear, ordered structure and makes related items easier to scan.
mistake: Alignment doesn't mean centring everything. Centred labels and fields leave ragged edges; give the labels a shared edge (left, or right so each sits against its box) and line the boxes up as well.

front: Contrast
back: Making elements clearly different, through colour, size, weight or shape, so that important items stand out and text is easy to read against its background.
mistake: Contrast isn't only about colour. Size, bold type and shape also create it, and colour alone fails users who can't tell some colours apart.

front: Navigation
back: How users find their way around a solution and move between its screens, using menus, tabs, links and Back and Next buttons. It works best when it is clear and predictable: each control keeps the same place, label and look on every screen, so users know where they are and how to move on or go back.
mistake: Consistency isn't one of the study design's design principles. Keeping the Back and Next buttons in the same place, with the same labels, on every screen is part of applying navigation.

front: How do design principles affect a solution's functionality, not just its appearance?
back: The study design groups its principles under functionality (interactivity, navigation), usability (ease of use, accessibility) and appearance. Clear navigation lets users reach each screen and move on without getting lost, and easy, accessible controls cut mistakes. Appearance principles help too: strong contrast keeps text readable, and aligned fields are faster to complete.

front: Light grey text on a white background has low {{contrast}}, so it is hard to read, especially for users with low vision.
back: Dark text on a light background, or light text on a dark one, raises contrast and keeps text readable in more conditions, such as on a phone in sunlight.

front: Contrast versus affordance
back:
| | Contrast | Affordance |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Belongs to | Design principles | Characteristics of user experience |
| About | How clearly elements differ in colour, size, weight or shape, so key items stand out and text is readable | Whether an element's appearance shows what it does and how to use it |
| Poor example | Pale grey text on a white background | Text that can be tapped but doesn't look like a button |
mistake: When users can't tell what a field or button is for, the problem is affordance, not contrast. A control can stand out strongly and still give no cue about how to use it.

front: Give an example of poor navigation in an interface and its effect on users.
back: The "Next" button sits bottom right on one screen and top left on the next, or is labelled "Continue" elsewhere. Users must search for the way forward on each screen, which slows them down and causes mistakes.

front: Why should the labels and text boxes on a data entry form be aligned?
back: Shared edges create clear columns, so the eye moves in a straight line down the form. Users find each field faster and can tell which label belongs to which box, and the form looks orderly.
